text.p: Industrial metals remained under pressure on Tuesday as investors reduced their exposure to the sector ahead of the traditionally slow summer quarter in the Northern Hemisphere. Not even a strike at the western world's biggest nickel producer could stem the flow of money out of the London Metal Exchange base metals' futures markets.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index fell 0.20 points to 248.44.

An early rally in several metals in a knee-jerk response to news of a strike at Canadian nickel/copper producer Inco Ltd was short-lived as investors hungrily sold into the higher levels. This soon turned prices lower, a trend which was aided by Russia's biggest nickel/copper producer, Norilsk, forecasting its 1997 output of the metals would rise by 20 percent and nine percent respectively. Nickel, after rallying $300 in early trade, fell back to settle at $7,180 at the end of the day.
By the end of the day the three months delivery copper prices had fallen to $2,479, having been above $2,500 earlier.
Aluminium traders reported an easing in recent tight supply pipelines and this contributed to an $18 fall to a six week low of $1,578 a tonne.

World oil markets fell on Tuesday amid reports that the United Nations was likely to extend its "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq and jitters ahead of the release of weekly U.S. stocks data. Brent Blend crude, the world benchmark grade, closed 62 cents down at $18.90 a barrel in London. It has averaged $19.39 in the past four months.
